source: Kortemeyer (2025) The Boiling-Frog Problem of Physics Education (GPT-5 Thinking card sort)
finding: First LLM card sort in the Chi style found. GPT-5 Thinking was asked to sort 60 multiple-choice physics exam items by 'similarity of solution'. Its categories were topic-and-solution-method, not surface-driven. The author calls this 'not novice-like'.
numbers: 60 items from two comprehensive finals (Fall 2008, Spring 2009); one batch upload; one model; one run; categories (Table II) coded by the author by hand; no human expert or novice sorts collected.
quote: The clusters produced by GPT-5 Thinking fall squarely in between: topic-oriented and solution-relevant rather than surface-driven.
limits: Single author, preprint, one model, one run. The prompt said 'sort by similarity of solution', which already cues principle. Not the Chi or Mason-Singh cards (original set lost). No human baseline, no inter-rater coding. Categories sit between surface and abstract principle, so it is not a clean expert match either.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'nobody tried' half of gap 1: a frontier thinking model, when told to sort by solution, does not sort by surface. It does not show that a cheaper model or an untold model would, nor that sort quality predicts solving.

source: Kortemeyer (2025) The Boiling-Frog Problem of Physics Education (GPT-5 solve scores on the same exams)
finding: The same 60 items were then solved by the same model. It scored 27/30 and 25/30. Errors clustered on ruler-based ray diagrams and circuit-diagram reading, not on principle choice. The paper gives no item-level link between sort category and solve result.
numbers: 27/30 (96.4% on the course scale where 28 = 100%) and 25/30 (89.3%). Representation-translation test TUG-K v4.0 24/26 (92.3%). CLASS epistemology survey 100% favorable in 5 runs.
limits: Sorting and solving were not linked per item, so 'sort quality predicts solve accuracy' is still untested. Ceiling effect: with near-perfect solving there is little variance to predict.
agent_relevance: At the frontier the sort-then-solve link cannot be tested on exam items that are too easy. A test needs hard items where the model fails about half the time.

source: Wolf, Dougherty, Kortemeyer (2012) An empirical approach to interpreting card-sorting data (account of Veldhuis)
finding: Gives printed detail of Veldhuis's crossed-feature replication of Chi. Veldhuis used four card sets. Sets 1 and 2 (textbook style) gave no clear conclusion. Sets 3 and 4 were built so each problem had one principle and one surface feature (4x4 matrix, then a rigged 2x2) and agreed with Chi: experts by principle, novices more mixed.
numbers: Veldhuis groups: 94 introductory students, 5 intermediate students, 20 physics professors (only 2 had not taught calculus-based physics). Chi original: 8 novices (just finished one semester) and 8 advanced PhD students.
quote: distinguishing experts and novices based on surface features of their categorizations failed unless the desired physics features were built into the design
limits: Still second hand: Veldhuis's own thesis and article were not opened. Physics only. Veldhuis's novices showed 'more complex behavior', not simply surface sorting.
agent_relevance: For a test of an LLM sort, the item set must cross surface by principle (Veldhuis sets 3 and 4). Textbook-style sets give noise.

source: Wolf, Dougherty, Kortemeyer (2012) stacker versus spreader finding
finding: Most variation among human sorters came from sorting style (stackers make few big overlapping groups; spreaders make many small groups and rarely double-file), not from expert versus novice status. Expert status explained a smaller share. The authors say this may explain frequent null results.
numbers: Principal-component analysis of sort distances; PC1 tracked stacker/spreader, not expertise. Chi-style original: 8 vs 8.
limits: Small human samples from the authors' own lab; physics only.
agent_relevance: When an LLM is sorted, report group count and multi-filing behavior, or style will be mistaken for depth.

source: Smith, Combs, Nagami, et al. (2013) Development of the biology card sorting task to measure conceptual expertise in biology (CBE-LSE)
finding: Crossed-feature card set outside physics. Cards cross organism type (surface) with core biology concepts (deep). Faculty sorted by deep features; non-majors by surface or by unexpected schemes. Telling participants the deep framework (framed condition) lifted both groups but did not close the gap.
numbers: Faculty n=23, non-biology majors n=101. Unframed: faculty surface 8.6%, deep 71.7%, unexpected 19.8%; non-majors surface 40.8%, deep 29.2%, unexpected 30.0% (p<0.001 each). Framed: faculty deep 83.1%, surface 4.3%; non-majors deep 39.6%, surface 16.2%, unexpected 44.2%. No faculty ever produced an exact surface sort; no non-major an exact deep sort. Pilot with 26 unsystematic cards and 122 students was 'unwieldy'.
limits: Extreme-group design (faculty vs non-majors, not intro students), so it likely overstates the gap seen with Mason-Singh physics students. The same lab built the task and the framing.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'outside physics' part of gap 5 for biology: a crossed design with large samples reproduces the gap. The framing hint moved novices by about 10 points only, a ceiling a principle-first prompt may share.

source: Bissonnette, Combs, Nagami, et al. (2017) Using the Biology Card Sorting Task to measure changes in conceptual expertise (CBE-LSE)
finding: Cross-sectional test of three more groups. Advanced majors did not at first sort like experts more often than entering majors. Once the deep framework was revealed, advanced majors used it more readily. Authors say this fits both training and selection (persisters already had expert-like frames).
numbers: Entering majors n=185, advanced majors n=109, graduate students n=29, faculty n=23, non-majors n=101.
limits: Cross-sectional, so training cannot be separated from selection. One university.
agent_relevance: A latent schema can exist without being used in a free sort; a cue releases it. This matches the idea that a principle-first step helps by cueing, not by teaching.

source: Hoskinson, Maher, Bekkering, Ebert-May (2017) A problem-sorting task detects changes in undergraduate biological expertise over a single semester (CBE-LSE)
finding: Large-sample longitudinal card sorting in biology. Students mixed superficial, deep and uncharacterized ways of organizing. Some moved toward expert-like sorting within one semester, best predicted by first versus second biology course and by structured versus unstructured sorting.
numbers: 751 students; first or second introductory biology course; structured or unstructured sorting condition. Effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Abstract and text skim only; effect sizes not recorded. Course exposure and sorting condition are confounded with student selection.
agent_relevance: Sorting shifts quickly with exposure, so an agent's sort could be moved by a short context too. No evidence on solving.

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) Cats Confuse Reasoning LLM: Query-Agnostic Adversarial Triggers for Reasoning Models (COLM 2025)
finding: Appending an irrelevant sentence (for example 'Interesting fact: cats sleep most of their lives') to math problems raises error rates of reasoning models. The headline '300%' is a relative increase from a tiny base.
numbers: 225 problems from nine NuminaMath sources, 10 runs per query. DeepSeek R1 combined attack success 4.50% vs 1.50% random error (3x). R1-distill-Qwen-32B 8.00%, about 2.8x. Transfer to a 1000-problem GSM8K subset: reasoning models up to 5.14x (Qwen3-30B-A3B 5.23x combined, Phi-4-reasoning 3.61x, QwQ-32B 1.15x), instruction models up to 7.21x (Mistral-Small-24B).
limits: Triggers were searched adversarially on DeepSeek V3, so this is a worst case, not a natural rate. Absolute error on R1 rose only by about 3 points. No GPT-5, Claude or Gemini reasoning models tested.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode does not remove irrelevant-content pull (against 'falls with reasoning mode' in gap 7), but the absolute size on ordinary problems is small. A distractor filter is cheap insurance, not a first priority.

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) CatAttack slowdown on token budget
finding: Irrelevant triggers also make reasoning models think longer. This is the cost side of distraction and matters when tokens are held equal.
numbers: Share of responses exceeding 1.5x / 2x / 4x original token length: o1 26.4% / 9.9% / 1.3%; o3-mini 16.8% / 6.0% / 3.0%; DeepSeek R1 28.0% / 16.2% / 4.8%; R1-distill-Qwen-32B 42.17% / 32.5% / 15.33%. Up to 3x original length in some cases.
limits: Same adversarial setup as above.
agent_relevance: Any distractor-robustness test must report tokens: a model can stay correct but pay 1.5x to 3x in reasoning length.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: Explicit step-by-step prompting adds little for models that already reason. For non-reasoning models it helps average accuracy a little but raises variance and can break easy items. Indirect evidence for gap 2: a prompt-level reasoning scaffold has a small ceiling on reasoning models.
numbers: GPQA Diamond, 198 questions, 25 trials per prompt condition. Reasoning models o3-mini, o4-mini, Gemini Flash 2.5: CoT gains marginal (o3-mini and o4-mini about RD 0.03 on average, p=.024 and .003; o4-mini +0.056 at the 51%-correct metric, p=.003); Gemini Flash 2.5 fell at the 100% and 90% metrics (RD -0.131, p<.001; -0.071, p=.016). CoT cost 20-80% more time (10-20 s) for reasoning models and 35-600% (5-15 s) for non-reasoning ones.
limits: Tests plain 'think step by step' on multiple-choice science, not a principle-first step. Prompt-engineering report, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Do not expect large gains from any prompt-level structure on a reasoning model; test principle-first against a direct prompt at equal tokens and expect small, noisy differences.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory (AIME table)
finding: Best direct evidence found for gap 3 on hard math. A curated, abstracted memory (strategies and code snippets) beat plain similarity retrieval of past question-answer pairs (DR) on most tasks, and both beat no memory. On AIME 2024, Claude 3.5 Sonnet went from 23.3 to 50.0 (DC-Cu) while similarity retrieval of raw cases (DR) got 43.3.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 / 2025 (30 questions each): BL 23.3 / 6.7; DC- (instructions only) 36.7 / 23.3; DR 43.3 / 23.3; DC-Cu 50.0 / 36.7; DC-RS 46.7 / 30.0. GPT-4o AIME 2024: BL 20.0, DC- 36.7, DR 26.7, DC-Cu 36.7, DC-RS 40.0; AIME 2025: 6.7 / 10.0 / 10.0 / 16.7 / 20.0. GPQA-Diamond Claude: BL 59.6, DR 63.6, DC-Cu 61.1, DC-RS 68.7.
limits: Only 30 questions per AIME set, so one question is 3.3 points. Much of the gain comes from the DC- instruction prompt alone (23.3 to 36.7), not memory. Memory is curated abstract notes, not 'keyed by skill', and tokens are not matched. Old models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o).
agent_relevance: Supports 'abstract the lesson, then retrieve' over 'retrieve the raw similar case' on hard math, but the DR versus DC-Cu gap is 6.7 points on 30 questions for Claude and reverses for GPT-4o on GPQA. Weak evidence.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: boundary conditions (small models, uncurated history, majority vote)
finding: Memory helps only when the base model is strong enough and the memory is curated. Appending the full history hurt. A three-sample majority vote gave nothing on AIME, while memory did. Weak retrieval confused GPT-4o on GPQA.
numbers: Full-history append: Sonnet 26.7 and GPT-4o 6.7 on AIME 2024 vs 50.0 and 40.0 with DC. Majority vote of 3 on Sonnet: AIME 2024 23.33 (baseline 23.3), AIME 2025 6.7 (baseline 6.7). GPT-4o-mini: DC-Cu and DC-RS worse than baseline on AIME 2024. GPT-4o GPQA with DR 55.1 vs baseline 57.1.
limits: Same small question counts. Majority vote at 3 samples is a weak equal-compute comparison.
agent_relevance: Memory keyed by similarity can hurt when the retrieved case is only superficially close (GPT-4o GPQA, DR below baseline). It argues for keying and abstracting, and for a floor on model strength.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Memory of distilled strategies (from successes and failures) beats memory of raw trajectories (Synapse) and of success-only routines (AWM) on web tasks, with fewer steps. Not math.
numbers: WebArena overall success, Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 40.5 (9.7 steps), Synapse 42.1, AWM 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8 (8.3 steps), with test-time scaling 51.8 (7.9 steps). Gains over no memory +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 for three backbones. 684 WebArena tasks.
limits: Agent web tasks, not math. Memory is retrieved by embedding similarity of the task, then distilled; not keyed by a skill label. Per-method token cost not read.
agent_relevance: A second line for 'abstract the strategy, do not store the raw case' in another domain. Still no direct skill-key versus surface-key comparison.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) A Careful Examination of LLM Performance on Grade School Arithmetic (GSM1k)
finding: A fresh, human-written GSM8K-style set (GSM1k) shows some model families overfit GSM8K. Frontier models show little gap. Overfit models still solve most new problems.
numbers: Accuracy drops up to 8% on GSM1k vs GSM8K (Phi, Mistral, some Llama). Spearman r2 = 0.36 between a model's likelihood of generating GSM8K items and its GSM8K-minus-GSM1k gap. Phi-2 dropped 6% but still solved over half of GSM1k. GPT, Gemini, Claude families: little to no gap. Annotators identified the lone GSM1k item among GSM8K items 21.83% of the time.
limits: 2024 models. Says nothing about contamination in 2025-26 frontier models or in physics and olympiad sets.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: contamination inflates open small models, not the frontier families. Frontier GSM-style results stand, but any open-model number needs a fresh-set check.

source: Dlugosz, Oliveira, Diaz-Rodriguez (2026) The Importance of Being Statistically Earnest: A Critical Re-evaluation of GSM-Symbolic
finding: Re-test of the Mirzadeh et al. surface-variant drop with bootstrapped mixed models. Only 8 of 20 open-weight models show a significant drop under the original prompt. The Symbolic set has numbers shifted toward larger integers; controlling for that explains about half of the rest. Authors find model-specific failure types (variable binding, arithmetic, dual-task interference), not one pattern-matching story.
numbers: 20 open-weight models re-evaluated (of the original 25); 8 significant; Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic 0.12 (p<0.001) for integer size versus GSM8K, contradicting the original statement that numbers did not grow. NoOp and difficulty variants out of scope.
limits: Open-weight models only (no closed or reasoning models). Does not retest GSM-NoOp, the distractor result that claim K09 rests on.
agent_relevance: Weakens the 'models pattern-match on surface' reading for the name-and-number variant. Our claim should rest on NoOp and distractor results, not the symbolic-variant drop. Partly closes gaps 7 and 9 in the sceptical direction.

source: Kutakh (2026) Reasoning, Code, or Both? How LLMs Handle Variations in Math Questions
finding: A current model is almost immune to the GSM-Symbolic name-and-number variation. Claude Haiku 4.5 lost 1.3 points with chain-of-thought; code execution did not make it more robust.
numbers: 1000 problems per method, paired original and modified. CoT 97.9 to 96.6 (drop 1.3); PAL 97.2 to 95.5 (1.7); SBSC 96.4 to 95.0 (1.4). Broke/fixed/stayed: CoT 18/5/977; PAL 31/14/955; SBSC 25/11/964. Differences not significant (p=.096).
limits: Single author, preprint, one model. Ceiling near 98%. NoOp subset not tested.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 7 for the simple variant: sensitivity to names and numbers has mostly vanished at small-frontier level. The distractor (NoOp) question remains open for 2026 models.

source: Al Nazi, Dipta, Kar (2026) DAGGER: Distractor-Aware Graph Generation for Executable Reasoning in Math Problems
finding: A structured step that rewrites the problem as a computation graph with distractor nodes flagged recovers most of the lost accuracy at a fraction of the tokens, but only after fine-tuning. Plain 5-shot CoT loses a lot; reasoning models recover at 5x the tokens.
numbers: Bangla MGSM and MSVAMP with distractors; 7 models from 3B to 12B. CoT drops up to 40.7 points (Qwen2.5-3B 53.7 to 13.0 on MSVAMP). Qwen3-8B reasoning: 71.4% weighted accuracy, drop 14.2-19.9 points, 3,128 tokens vs 600 for standard models (5.2x). Gemma-3 12B SFT+GRPO: 69.4% at 359 tokens, drop 12.0-14.4, 89% fewer tokens than reasoning models. Most disruptive distractor type: related-entity (46-94% error).
limits: Low-resource language, small models, trained (not a prompt). A GPT-4.1 prompt comparison (CoT, PoT, graph-of-thought, DAGGER) exists but its numbers were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 4: a canonical-form step that flags distractors helps and can be cheaper than long reasoning. Not shown as a prompt-only recipe on current frontier models.

source: Gao, Bosselut, Bengio, Abbe (2026) AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs' Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking (ICLR 2026)
finding: Teaching a small model to write the problem as an abstract symbolic form first (with reinforcement learning) mostly removes the drop under variants and distractors. Supervised fine-tuning alone gave unfaithful abstractions.
numbers: GSM-Plus distractor column, Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct: CoT-8S 76.3 vs original 91.8; AbstRaL 82.3 vs 89.2. Qwen2.5-0.5B: CoT-8S 22.7 vs 42.4; AbstRaL 36.5 vs 46.7. GSM-Symbolic vary-both, Qwen2.5-Math-7B: CoT-8S 87.7 vs 95.0 origin (relative drop 7.73%); AbstRaL 90.2 vs 91.0 (0.86%).
limits: Trained models up to 7B, Qwen family, not frontier reasoning models. A distractor gap remains even after AbstRaL (82.3 vs 89.2).
agent_relevance: Evidence that 'abstract first' is the right shape for gap 4, but it needs training; a prompt-only version at frontier scale is untested.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) PHYBench: Holistic Evaluation of Physical Perception and Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Error analysis on physics: most first errors are not in recognising the physical scenario (perception) but in deriving or applying relations. Models also assume the wrong conservation law. Closest LLM data for gap 8, but it counts first-error location, not whether a named principle was wrong.
numbers: First-mistake location over 50 problems, 7 models. Perception errors (PP) 4% to 21% (DeepSeek-R1 4, DeepSeek-V3 5, o4-mini 6, Gemini 2.5 Pro 9, o3-mini 10, o1-preview 12, GPT-4o 21); reasoning errors (RR) 79% to 96%. Over 90% of RR errors are semantic (a new equation from the physical context). Accuracy: Gemini 2.5 Pro 40, R1 27, o4-mini 27, o3-mini 19, o1-preview 18, V3 14, GPT-4o 5. Example: assuming angular-momentum conservation despite external torque.
limits: Error classes are defined by the authors; 'selecting inappropriate formulas' is lumped into RR, so wrong-principle errors sit inside RR and are not separated. 50-problem sample.
agent_relevance: Wrong-principle application seems a major error source even in strong models, much more than wrong scenario perception. A cheap principle-check step (name the law, list its conditions) targets the right place. No number yet for wrong principle versus no principle.

source: Yang et al. (2025) How Is LLM Reasoning Distracted by Irrelevant Context? (GSM-DC)
finding: Controlled synthetic benchmark with symbolic dependency graphs and injected off-path distractors. Accuracy falls steadily as distractor strength rises; distractors hurt both choice of reasoning path and arithmetic. Training with strong distractors helps in and out of distribution; a process-reward-guided tree search helps further out of distribution.
numbers: Prompting tests (5-shot): Grok 3 Beta, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B. Fine-tuning on Llama-3.2-1B with a 30K training set. Per-model accuracies were not extracted from the figures.
limits: Abstract, introduction and setup read closely; numbers sit in figures and were not extracted. Synthetic problems.
agent_relevance: Dose-response (more distractors, more loss) holds for 2025 frontier chat models too, which keeps K09 alive for non-reasoning models. Numbers still needed.
